title: Bachitar Natak
hook: his autobiographical poem, the wondrous drama

segments.voice: Yesterday, sparks from one fire: beings rise from the One like sparks, and fall back into it. Your line was sparks of one fire. Who did you see as a spark off the same fire? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.

Celebrity memoirs tend to open the same way. A childhood street. A first big break. A photo section in the middle. Readers come for the person, and the book obliges: me, my story, my wins. Now a different kind of life story. Its author was a Guru, a poet and a leader of armies. He had plenty of wins to tell. And he chose to call his own story a drama, a wondrous one, and to open it somewhere else entirely.
screen: `ME, MY STORY, MY WINS.` → `A GURU WRITES HIS LIFE.` → `HE CALLS IT A DRAMA.`

segments.voice: Bachitar Natak: the wondrous drama. It's a long poem in the Dasam Granth, and in it Guru Gobind Singh tells parts of his own story in his own voice. Here, the tenth Guru says I. But look where it begins. Not with a birth, not with a battle. It opens with praise. It bows, in paraphrase, to the holy sword, and to the Timeless One whom the poet sees in the sword's strength, the One who cuts down wrong and protects the good. The praise goes on at length before the poet says much about himself at all. Then the story widens before it narrows. He tells of an ancient lineage, the old families that, tradition says, the Gurus' line came from. He tells of a life before this life: a time of deep meditation in the mountains, absorbed in the One, until he was called and sent into the world, to stand up for dharma, for what is right. Only then does he arrive at his birth. So why a drama? A drama is a play with a director. The actors are real, the danger is real, the costumes are real, but someone else wrote the play. The Guru tells his life as a scene inside God's larger play. The wonder isn't him. The wonder is the play he found himself sent into. That frames everything this block will read in Bachitar Natak in the next few days: what he says about himself, a battle he fought, and his father. All of it told by someone who begins with praise and sees himself as a part in the play.
screen: `THE TENTH GURU SAYS I.` · `IT OPENS WITH PRAISE.` · `A LIFE BEFORE, AND A CALLING.` · `A SCENE IN GOD'S PLAY.` · then, large: `THE WONDROUS DRAMA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read its opening, or begin your own story the way it does. Settle, and breathe. If you were to tell your life in one page, what would the first line be? Let the usual answers come: where you were born, what you've done. Then try another opening. Start with what holds you. Thanks, or wonder, or the people who carried you before you could walk. Let your story be one scene in something larger. Later today, look up the opening of Bachitar Natak in a translation and read a few lines. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Bachitar Natak. The wondrous drama: Guru Gobind Singh's poem about his own life, which opens with praise and tells his story as one scene in God's play. Today's word.
Your line: the wondrous drama. Today, when your part feels heavy, remember that it's one scene in a larger play. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs read Bachitar Natak as Guru Gobind Singh's own account of his calling and his early life, and passages from it are told in katha on gurpurabs and at historical gurdwaras.
